student_passage:
Reading the Wind

[A] My cousin Tessa invited me to help a coastal weather club launch what she called an instrument kite. I pictured a bright toy tugging uselessly above the beach and wondered why the club did not simply use instead a regular ordinary weather station[1]. On the sand, however, the kite looked less like a toy than a narrow white wing. A small sensor package hung beneath its line.

[B] Club leader Ren Ito lifted a handful of sand and let it stream between his fingers. Farther inland, the grains fell almost straight down; near the water, they moved like smoke being pulled through an invisible doorway[2]. Ito explained that wind can change with height. The club members checked the kite's seams and returned its[3] tools to a shared case before carrying the wing toward the open beach.

Tessa tied three short ribbons along the line so the team could see small changes in airflow.[4] Watching the ribbons flatten toward the dunes, the launch direction was changed by Ito.[5] He asked us to turn until the wind struck the wing evenly. Tessa held the frame upright while I released more line. [C]

The first launch ended quickly. One side of the kite dipped, it dragged[6] a wingtip through the sand. Ito shortened a bridle cord by two centimeters, changing the angle at which the line pulled the frame. Tessa raises[7] the kite again. This time it climbed steadily, carrying the sensor above the warm air close to the beach and into the cooler flow overhead.

At first, every knot and adjustment had seemed fussy to me. Gradually, however, the movements of the ribbons, wing, and line began to look like readable evidence rather than delay.[8] [D] Before the launch, Ito had explained that the sensor would record temperature and wind speed at several heights.[9] When the kite returned, its measurements showed the temperature falling as it climbed. I had arrived expecting to watch a toy fly. I left understanding that the kite was a carefully balanced question sent upward—and that the wind answered through every change in its motion.[10]
